restatements.text: Requires cities to allow up to two homes on lots zoned for single-family residential use and prohibits cities from requiring a public hearing to approve projects that meet this requirement.

findings.quote: A city shall allow up to two homes on any lot zoned for single-family residential use. A city may not require a public hearing to approve a project that meets this section.
findings.mechanism: It increases the number of homes permitted on single-family lots and bans public hearing requirements for these projects, making the housing approval process easier.

findings.quote: A city shall allow up to two homes on any lot zoned for single-family residential use.
findings.mechanism: It preempts local authority by setting a statewide rule for the minimum number of homes cities must allow on residential lots.

findings.quote: A city may not require a public hearing to approve a project that meets this section.
findings.mechanism: It prohibits cities from holding public hearings for qualifying housing projects, removing a channel for open meetings and public oversight of the approval process.

findings.quote: A city shall allow up to two homes on any lot zoned for single-family residential use.
findings.mechanism: It expands property owners' control over their land by granting them the right to build a second home on lots previously restricted to a single home.

analysis.answer: Currently, cities have the authority to determine how many homes can be built on each residential lot. This measure changes that by requiring all cities to allow up to two homes on any lot zoned for single-family use and by forbidding them from requiring a public hearing to approve such projects.

Direct costs for municipalities include the administrative work to update their zoning codes and approval processes. Opportunity costs and compliance costs decrease for developers and property owners, who save the time and expense associated with preparing for and attending public hearings.

Property owners benefit by gaining the option to build a second unit. Developers and builders benefit from expanded building opportunities and streamlined approvals. Local governments bear a loss of zoning authority, and residents of single-family neighborhoods bear the loss of a public forum to oppose nearby developments.

Property owners are incentivized to build duplexes or accessory dwelling units on single-family lots to increase property value or generate rental income. Cities might respond by adjusting other, non-preempted zoning rules (such as setback requirements or height limits) to retain some control over the scale of new projects.

The measure addresses housing shortages attributed to restrictive local zoning. By preempting local single-family zoning limits and removing public hearings, the mechanism directly targets development bottlenecks, lowering entry barriers to building while bypassing local community opposition.

State lawmakers gain authority at the expense of city councils and local planning boards. Property owners gain discretion over the development of their lots, while neighborhood groups lose a venue (public hearings) to exert influence over nearby projects.

Researchers generally agree that removing single-family zoning restrictions and streamlining approvals increases overall housing supply. However, they disagree on the extent to which this new supply trickles down to lower costs for middle- and lower-income renters, versus primarily benefiting property owners, developers, and higher-income buyers.
